An Apple user in California has filed a class-action lawsuit accusing the company of misleading consumers about the privacy protections of its "Hide My Email" feature. The details of the incident are as follows.

Apple sued over alleged flaw in Hide My Email feature

Recently, 404 Media reported that Apple was aware of a potential vulnerability more than a year ago that could leak the real email addresses behind "Hide My Email" aliases.

Apple's "Hide My Email" feature allows users to create unique, randomly generated email addresses that forward messages to their personal inboxes, enabling users to sign up for apps, websites, and newsletter subscriptions without revealing their real addresses.

Users can access this feature for free through "Sign in with Apple," while the iCloud+ plan (starting at US$0.99 per month) includes a more feature-rich version that lets users create aliases for websites, newsletters, and other services.

According to 404 Media, a security researcher alerted Apple in June 2025 about the vulnerability that could leak the real email addresses behind "Hide My Email" aliases.

Apple acknowledged receiving the report about a month later, but allegedly failed to address the issue. In March 2026, the company said it had fixed the flaw, but the researcher found the vulnerability could still be exploited.

Returning to the lawsuit itself (as reported by MacRumors), plaintiff Anthony Alvarez stated:

Apple was aware of the issue more than a year ago, yet the vulnerability remains unfixed — meanwhile, Apple continues to profit from "Hide My Email" and its privacy promises. The plaintiff is one of millions of customers who pay for iCloud+ and trust that Apple's "Hide My Email" will protect their personal email addresses. Plaintiffs and class members have paid for privacy — iCloud+ users through the premium baked into their iCloud+ subscription fees, and all Apple customers through the premium included in Apple's product pricing, which Apple marketed as featuring enhanced privacy protections and features such as "Hide My Email."

The lawsuit also claims this is not an isolated incident, citing a 2023 report that Apple's MAC address randomization feature could leak users' real hardware identifiers.

The complaint also alleges that the total amount of claims by class members exceeds US$5 million (excluding interest and legal fees), but does not explain how that figure was calculated.

Alvarez filed the lawsuit on behalf of himself and other Apple customers allegedly affected in the same way. He is asking the court to certify the case as a class action covering four proposed user groups:

  • All Apple customers nationwide who purchased a device and used "Hide My Email";
  • The above users in the California district;
  • All iCloud+ subscribers nationwide who have used the feature;
  • iCloud+ subscribers in the California district.

He is requesting a jury trial and, in addition to monetary damages in an amount to be determined, is asking the court to order Apple to fix "Hide My Email" or clearly disclose its limitations.

Apple has not yet responded to the lawsuit.
